name: Digital Literacy Basics
objectives: Given where you live, find a free or low-cost way to get online and list the safety steps for public Wi-Fi and shared computers, naming at least one real place or program and at least two safety steps
Using a search engine, search for the official page of a service you need using clear key words, reaching the official page while skipping any ads

Given an online form on an official site, fill in the form correctly and save proof that you sent it, with every required field filled in and the confirmation saved

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Finding information you can trust

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Getting connected for free or low cost
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a free or low-cost way to get online near you.
This lesson builds toward: Given where you live, you will find a free or low-cost way to get online and list the safety steps for public Wi-Fi and shared computers, naming at least one real place or program and at least two safety steps.
You do not need your own computer to get online. Public libraries usually have free computers, free Wi-Fi and staff who help. Many job centers, reentry and community centers also have computer labs.
Lifeline is a federal program, overseen by the FCC, that gives a monthly discount on phone or internet service to people who qualify, usually by income or by being in a program such as SNAP or Medicaid. The discount amount can change, so check lifelinesupport.org for the current amount and how to apply.
On public Wi-Fi, stick to websites that start with https and show a lock, and avoid banking on shared computers. Always sign out and close the browser when you finish on a shared computer.
Step by step:
- Search for your nearest public library and check its hours.
- Ask staff about free computers, Wi-Fi and help sessions.
- If cost is a problem, read about Lifeline at lifelinesupport.org.
- On shared computers, sign out and close the browser when done.
Words to know:
- Wi-Fi: a wireless internet connection.
- Lifeline: a federal program that lowers the monthly cost of phone or internet service for people who qualify.
- https: the start of a website address that means the connection is encrypted (scrambled).
Official sources:
- Lifeline Support (USAC, for the FCC)
Try it now: Find your nearest public library online. Write down its address, its hours and whether it offers free computer help.
You can now find a free or low-cost way to get online and use shared computers safely.

check.q: Which program gives a monthly discount on phone or internet service to people who qualify?
check.why: Lifeline is a federal program, overseen by the FCC, that lowers phone or internet costs.

check.q: You finish checking your email on a library computer. What would you do before you leave?
options: Leave the browser open for the next person
Save your password in the browser
Sign out and close the browser
Write your password on a sticky note
check.why: Signing out and closing the browser stops the next person from getting into your account.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Searching well
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a search engine to find a specific official page quickly.
This lesson builds toward: Using a search engine, you will search for the official page of a service you need using clear key words, reaching the official page while skipping any ads.
A search engine, such as Google or Bing, finds web pages for the words you type. Use a few clear key words, not a full story: "California DMV renew ID" works better than "how do I get my ID back I lost it last year".
Add your state or city to get local results. Put words in quotation marks to find that exact phrase. Add "site:.gov" to see only US government websites.
The top results are often ads, marked "Sponsored" or "Ad". Ads can be fake or can charge you for something that is free on the official site. Scroll past them to the real results.
Step by step:
- Type 3 to 6 key words.
- Add your state or city.
- Add site:.gov for government pages.
- Skip results marked Sponsored or Ad.
- Open the result and read the web address before you trust it.
Words to know:
- Search engine: a website that finds web pages for the words you type, like Google or Bing.
- Key words: the most important words for what you want to find.
- Sponsored / Ad: a paid result, not always the official or best one.
Try it now: Search for your state's job center or unemployment office. Try once with a long sentence and once with key words plus site:.gov. Which search found the official page faster?
You can now search with key words, skip ads, and find official pages quickly.

check.q: What does putting words in quotation marks do in a search?
check.why: Quotation marks tell the search engine to find the exact phrase.

check.q: You need to renew your ID in your state. Which search would you type?
options: Your state's name, "renew ID" and site:.gov
"I lost my ID last year and I do not know what to do"
check.why: A few clear key words, your state and site:.gov lead to the official page.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Is it true? Checking information
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide whether a website or post can be trusted before you act on it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a website or post, you will check whether the information can be trusted using the four questions, answering who made it, when, what other trusted sources say and whether it rushes you.
Anyone can post anything online. Before you trust it, ask four questions. Who made it? Look at the web address and the "About" page; US government sites end in .gov. When was it written? Rules and prices change. What do other trusted sources say? Check at least one more. Does it try to rush or scare you? That is a warning sign.
Watch for look-alike addresses, like a site that adds extra words or changes one letter of a real name. Watch for photos and videos made or changed with AI; if a picture seems shocking, search for it in news from trusted outlets before sharing.
False information that spreads by mistake is called misinformation. False information spread on purpose is called disinformation. Do not share something until you have checked it.
Step by step:
- Who made it? Read the address and the About page.
- When? Find the date.
- Who else says so? Check one more trusted source.
- Is it rushing or scaring you? Slow down.
- Do not share until you have checked.
Words to know:
- Source: where information comes from.
- Misinformation: false information shared by mistake.
- Disinformation: false information spread on purpose.
- Look-alike site: a fake website with an address made to look like a real one.
Try it now: Find a post or article about a benefit, a job program or a health tip. Answer the four questions about it and decide: trust it, check more, or ignore it.
You can now check whether online information is trustworthy before you act on it or share it.

options: False information that spreads by mistake
An ad at the top of a search
check.why: Misinformation is false information spread by mistake; on purpose it is disinformation.

check.q: A message links to a job site whose address changes one letter of a well-known company's name. What would you do?
options: Assume it is fine because it looks the same
Treat it as a likely fake and go to the real site another way
check.why: Look-alike addresses are a warning sign of a fake site.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting things done online safely

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Filling out online forms
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Fill out an online form correctly and save proof you sent it.
This lesson builds toward: Given an online form on an official site, you will fill in the form correctly and save proof that you sent it, with every required field filled in and the confirmation saved.
Before you start, gather what the form will ask for: your contact details, dates, work or address history, and any document you need to upload. Have an email address you check often, because most sites send confirmations there.
Fields marked with a star (*) are required. Use the Tab key to move to the next box on a computer. Read every drop-down menu and check box. Many long forms let you save and come back; write down where to log back in.
Before you press Submit, review every page. After you submit, save the confirmation: take a screenshot, download the PDF, or write down the confirmation number. Only type ID numbers into the official site, never into a site you reached from an ad or a text.
Step by step:
- Make sure you are on the official site.
- Gather the details and documents first.
- Fill in required fields (*); use Tab to move.
- Save your progress on long forms.
- Review every page, then Submit.
- Save the confirmation number or screenshot.
Words to know:
- Field: one box on a form where you type an answer.
- Required (*): a field you must fill in before you can submit.
- Confirmation number: a code that proves your form was received.
- Drop-down menu: a box that opens a list to choose from.
Try it now: Find a practice or contact form on an official site, such as your library's "Ask a librarian" form. Fill it in up to the Submit button without sending, and point out the required fields.
You can now fill out an online form correctly and keep proof you sent it.

check.q: Why have an email address you check often before you fill in forms?
options: Forms will not open without one
Most sites send confirmations to your email
check.why: Most sites send confirmations and updates to your email.

check.q: You reach the last page of a benefits application. What would you do before pressing Submit?
check.why: Reviewing every page catches mistakes before you send it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Scanning and uploading documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Scan a paper document with a phone and save it as a PDF with a clear name.
This lesson builds toward: Given a paper document and a phone, you will scan the document and save it as a PDF with a clear file name, with a flat, readable scan and a name that says whose document it is and what it is.
Many forms ask you to upload documents: a résumé, a letter, proof of address. You can scan with a phone. On an iPhone, the Notes app and the Files app have a scan option. On Android, the Google Drive app has a Scan button. Look for a camera or scan icon.
For a good scan: lay the paper flat on a dark surface, use good light, hold the phone straight above it, and let the app crop the edges. Save it as a PDF.
Name the file clearly, like "Jordan-Lee-Resume-2026.pdf", not "IMG_2034". Only upload ID or private documents to official sites, and delete copies from shared or library computers when you finish.
Step by step:
- Open a scan tool: Notes or Files (iPhone), Google Drive (Android).
- Lay the page flat in good light.
- Hold the phone straight above it and scan.
- Save as PDF with a clear file name.
- Upload only on the official site; delete copies from shared computers.
Words to know:
- Scan: make a clear digital copy of a paper page.
- Upload: send a file from your device to a website.
- File name: the name a file is saved with, which helps you and others find it.
Try it now: Scan one practice page (a letter you wrote, not a real ID) with your phone. Save it as a PDF and give it a clear file name.
You can now scan a paper document with a phone and save it as a clearly named PDF ready to upload.

check.q: Which file name is best for an uploaded letter?
check.why: A clear name says whose document it is and what it is.

check.q: You scanned a document on a library computer and uploaded it. What would you do next?
options: Leave it in the Downloads folder
Delete the copies from the computer
Email it to everyone you know
check.why: Delete copies of private documents from shared or library computers when you finish.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your digital footprint and privacy
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check and tighten what others can see about you online.
This lesson builds toward: Using a search engine and your social media settings, you will check what others can see about you online and tighten your privacy settings, with your own name searched and at least one privacy setting changed.
Your digital footprint is everything about you online: posts, photos, comments, and what others post about you. Employers, landlords and schools often search a person's name. Posts can stay online even after you delete them, because others can screenshot or share them.
Search your own name in a search engine and see what comes up. In each social media app, open the settings and look for Privacy. Choose who can see your posts, who can tag you and whether strangers can message you.
Think before you post: would you be comfortable if a future boss, your family or your parole or probation officer saw it? Do not post your address, travel plans, ID documents or anything that could be used to pretend to be you.
Step by step:
- Search your full name in quotes.
- Open each social app's Privacy settings.
- Limit who can see posts, tag you and message you.
- Remove or hide posts you would not want an employer to see.
- Think before every new post.
Words to know:
- Digital footprint: everything about you that is online, posted by you or by others.
- Privacy settings: choices in an app about who can see your information.
- Tag: linking a person's name or account to a post or photo.
Try it now: Final task: find the official site for a service you need and prove it is official, find its form or steps, scan a practice page to a clearly named PDF, then search your own name and tighten one privacy setting.
You can now get a real task done online while keeping your private information and reputation safe.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Finding the official site The site found is an ad, a look-alike or not the right service. The official site for the service is found by search, skipping the ads. Also finds the exact page with the form or steps in a few clicks. Checking the site No reason is given for trusting the site. Shows how the site was checked, such as a .gov address and the About page. Also checks a second trusted source or the date the page was updated. Scan and file name The scan is blurred or cut off, or the file is named like IMG_2034. A clear PDF scan of a practice document with a clear file name. The scan is cropped neatly and copies are deleted from any shared computer. Keeping private information safe A real ID was scanned, or the three lines say nothing about privacy. Three lines explain how the site was checked and how private information was kept safe. Also names one privacy setting checked or changed on a social media app. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why can a post stay online after you delete it?
options: Others may have taken a screenshot or shared it
Deleting never works on any app
check.why: Other people can screenshot or share a post before you delete it.

check.q: Strangers keep messaging you on a social media app. What would you do?
options: Post your address so they know you
Open the app's Privacy settings and limit who can message you
check.why: Privacy settings let you choose who can message you, see your posts and tag you.
